newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Speculation swirls ahead of SAirGroup briefing.
newsitem.headline: Speculation swirls ahead of SAirGroup briefing.

text.p: SAirGroup's recent announcement of a large, but unspecified provision "for future structural adjustments" has triggered intense speculation that the Swiss airline group is planning another bold strategic move.

Scenarios range from a merger or a sale of the core Swissair airline to new alliances, while other explanations include a new round of layoffs, restructuring, general loss-provisions or changes to the European route network or fleet.
On Friday the rumour mill grinds to a halt as SAirGroup lifts the veil of secrecy at its annual news conference.

The charge was announced on April 4 when SAirGroup released 1996 results, including a 300 million Swiss francs ($204.2 million) provision for "future structural adjustments to the full liberalisation of the European air transport market from April 1, 1997."

SAirGroup also took a 267 million franc charge for writing down the value of its stake in partner Sabena SA so it ended with a larger-than-expected 1996 net loss of 497 million francs after a 40 percent rise in operating profit to 344 million.
The provision puzzled analysts, but neither SAirGroup's press office nor its chief executive Philippe Bruggisser have revealed what it covers.
The standard answer to journalists as well as industry analysts has been: "Wait until April 18."

The only clue in the news release was that the "provisions should create a sound foundation for further enhancing the SAirGroup's ability to compete in the newly-liberalised European air transport market."
Swiss daily newspaper Tages-Anzeiger concluded that hundreds of jobs would be cut.
Unions, however, doubt this scenario.
"We haven't been informed about any measures," said a spokesman for the VPOD union, which represents ground staff.

Neither VPOD, which represents ground staff, or Aeropers, the pilots' union, are in talks with SAirGroup management and new layoffs are not considered likely as the last round of 2,000 job cuts is still being carried out.
"The workforce has been cut so much that further cuts would involve a resizing of Swissair or a massive reduction in service levels, something noone wants," the VPOD spokesman added.

Despite the large net loss, the stock market welcomed the higher-than-expected 1996 operating profit and the write-off of Sabena, which should wipe the slate clean and lay the ground for a significant profit recovery in 1997.
SAirGroup's share has gained 67 francs ($45.61), or 5.5 percent since its results were announced and risen 19.7 percent since the start of 1997.

The rise in SAirGroup's share price this year has been helped by expectations the Swissair airline at some point will merge or enter into an alliance with a major carrier -- Deutsche Lufthansa AG is a perennial favourite -- when consolidation in Europe's airline sector gathers pace.
The unspecified provisions added fuel to this speculation.
The European shakeout, however, has not yet really begun and most analysts first expected the issue of mergers or new alliances to move to the front burner in a few years.

Despite its European alliance with Austrian Airlines and Sabena SA, Swissair's lack of a large domestic market is seen as a critical weakness when comparing its future chance of survival with that of Air France or Deutsche Lufthansa AG.
Another reason that SAirGroup is likely to wait with stategic decisions about Swissair is that it is still a loss-making airline and that weakens any barganing position.
A further reason is that one of Bruggisser's prime goals is for Swissair's flight operations to break even by year-end.
Given Bruggisser's oft-repeated commitment to this goal, analysts expect that he dearly wants to achieve that before giving up and looking at other options.
-- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340 ($ = 1.468 Swiss Francs)
